```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Every number of the expected-numbers section is read from the committed data
# files of the case, so that the guide and the pages cannot drift apart: with
# readr rather than datawizard::data_read(), which reads empty cells as "" and
# the codes of the cases, strata and clusters as numbers.
data_dir <- "../cases/cohabitation/data"
fmt <- \(x, d = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
big <- \(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
sgn <- \(x, d = 3) paste0(dplyr::if_else(x > 0, "+", ""), fmt(x, d))
pct <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(fmt(100 * x, d), "%")
pe <- \(p) if (p < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else paste("p =", fmt(p, 3))

unions <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "cohab_unions.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                          col_types = readr::cols(caseid = readr::col_character(),
                                                  stratum = readr::col_character(),
                                                  psu = readr::col_character()))
score <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "score_person_months.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
curve <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "spec_curve.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                         col_types = readr::cols(stat_type = readr::col_character()))
analysts <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "analysts5.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
marks <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "reference_marks.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
deviations <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "menu_deviations.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
inference <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "display_inference.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                             col_types = readr::cols(stat_type = readr::col_character()))
options_d <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "display_options.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE,
                             col_types = readr::cols(stat_type = readr::col_character()))
repro <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "display_reproduction.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
subgroups <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "display_subgroups.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
lifetable <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "display_lifetable.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

ref <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
an <- \(id, col) analysts[[col]][analysts$id == id]
mark <- \(id, col = "b") marks[[col]][marks$mark == id]
shift <- \(axis, option, col = "shift_mean") deviations[[col]][deviations$axis == axis & deviations$option == option]
inf <- \(rule, col) inference[[col]][inference$errors == rule]
opt <- \(changed, option, col = "b") options_d[[col]][options_d$changed == changed & options_d$option == option]
sg <- \(model, group) subgroups$b[subgroups$model == model & subgroups$group == group]
by_set <- curve |> datawizard::data_summary(mean = mean(b), by = "adjust")
bs <- \(set) by_set$mean[by_set$adjust == set]

# The unions of the paper, as spec_unions() of the workspace keeps them, and
# their weighted composition
paper <- unions |>
  datawizard::data_filter(cycle %in% c("1995", "2006-10"), since_start <= 60, !is.na(duration), duration >= 1,
                          cycle != "2006-10" | from_2005)
oc <- \(cycle, outcome) sum(paper$cycle == cycle & paper$outcome == outcome)
share <- \(cycle, test) {
  rows <- paper[paper$cycle == cycle, ]
  stats::weighted.mean(test(rows), rows$weight)
}
lt36 <- datawizard::data_filter(lifetable, group_type == "all", month == 36)

# The rows and the unions of the file that Multi100 gave the analysts
score_rows <- score |>
  datawizard::data_filter(P95 == 1 | P10 == 1) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(rows = n(), married = sum(OUTCOME == 2), by = "P95")
sr <- \(p95, col) score_rows[[col]][score_rows$P95 == p95]
score_unions <- score |>
  datawizard::data_filter(P95 == 1 | P10 == 1) |>
  dplyr::slice_max(MONTHNUM, n = 1, by = CASEID) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(survey = dplyr::if_else(P95 == 1, "1995", "2006-10"),
                          outcome = c("intact", "marriage", "separation")[OUTCOME])
su <- \(survey, outcome) sum(score_unions$survey == survey & score_unions$outcome == outcome)
in_file <- paper |>
  datawizard::data_filter(cycle == "1995") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(in_score = caseid %in% as.character(score_unions$CASEID))
kept <- \(outcome) sum(in_file$outcome == outcome & in_file$in_score)
# The same test without the continuity correction, a usual departure
chi_uncorrected <- unname(stats::prop.test(x = c(sr(1, "married"), sr(0, "married")),
                                           n = c(sr(1, "rows"), sr(0, "rows")), correct = FALSE)$statistic)

# Placement as try_spec() prints it: the specifications further below zero
placement <- \(b) sum(curve$b < b - 1e-9)
five_years_ref <- curve |>
  datawizard::data_filter(cohorts == "five_years", horizon == "five_years", adjust == "composition",
                          weights == "weighted", time == "linear", model == "mlogit")
# The share of the variance of the 144 estimates carried by each decision: its
# eta squared in a main-effects model (effectsize), the sum of squares of the
# decision over the total
var_eta <- stats::lm(b ~ cohorts + horizon + adjust + weights + time + model, data = curve) |>
  effectsize::eta_squared(partial = FALSE, ci = NULL)
var_part <- \(term) var_eta$Eta2[var_eta$Parameter == term]
```

::: {.callout-note}
**This document is for the facilitator.** It is rendered with the site but left out of the navbar, so nothing on the site links to it. It holds the run sheet of the one-day course on the cohabitation case (deck `slides/cohabitation-one-day.qmd`), the checks before a delivery, the two moments of Task 3 that the day is built around, the expected numbers and the fallbacks. The participant pages under `tracks/cohabitation-one-day/` carry the same timings without the instructor guidance.
:::

## The delivery lifecycle {#delivery-lifecycle}

Between deliveries the opening page advertises no delivery. Scheduling one takes three steps, and resetting after one takes two.

**Scheduling.**

- [ ] Fill the `delivery:` block in `_variables.yml` (date, venue, event, mode, registration URL), set `track: cohabitation-one-day`, and set `active: 'true'`. Render the opening page (`quarto render index.qmd`), and it shows a "Next delivery" callout with a link to the track. Set `active: 'false'` again afterwards.
- [ ] Decide on recording. If you record, record the talk only, announce it at the start of each recorded stretch, and pause it for the hands-on tasks. Nothing in the day depends on the recording either way.
- [ ] Decide which way the day leans. The deck keeps two kinds of optional run on the `d` key: `tools` (five slides in the tools segment of Part 1 and the nine-slide R tutorial of Part 2) and `methods` (the five-slide tutorial on person-period data and discrete-time models in Part 3 and the two slides of multiverse background in Part 4). To make a run part of the main flow, list it under `core-runs:` in the YAML of `slides/cohabitation-one-day.qmd` and render the deck again; a run that is not listed stays optional and can still be switched on live. For a class of demographers the `methods` run is the one to drop first, and for a class that has never met event-history data it is the one to keep.

**Resetting, before the next delivery.**

- [ ] Export the responses Sheet (File → Download → CSV) and keep it as a dated snapshot, for example `cases/cohabitation/data/class_results_2026-11-20.csv`.
- [ ] Clear the rows of earlier deliveries from the Sheet, so that the chart opens almost empty for the next class, but only once no other case is collecting results in it (see the Form below). Do not touch the Form, the Worker or the field schema; only the rows change from one class to the next.

---

## Before the day

### The week before

- [ ] **The workspace repository.** The pages of the case are part of the course site (`CodeMoreh/applied-replication`), but the workspace (`CodeMoreh/replication-lab-cohabitation`) does not exist on GitHub yet, and every address that points at it is a placeholder until it does: the workspace zip on the setup page and the cheatsheet, the workspace address on the tools slide of Part 1, and the links in the README of the workspace. Create the repository, push it, and download the zip once from its public address to confirm that it unzips into `replication-lab-cohabitation-main`.
- [ ] **The class-results Form.** Out of the box, the helpers of the case submit to the results Form that every case shares, the one set up for the EU-frames case. Every label of this case reads `explore: [tag] cohabitation …` or `declared: [tag] cohabitation …`, and the class chart on the [Multiverse](../cases/cohabitation/multiverse.qmd#class-results) page keeps only the rows whose label carries the word `cohabitation` after the tag. That works as it stands. Clear the Sheet of the rows of earlier deliveries before the day (the data rows below the header of the tab "Form Responses 1"; the Form keeps working), because the EU-frames chart reads every row and would draw cohabitation rows as unclassed diamonds. The alternative, which keeps the classes of the cases apart for good, is a Form of its own, about twenty minutes once, following `facilitator/live-results-setup.md`: copy the Form, link a new Sheet, deploy a second Worker, and wire the new codes into the configuration blocks of `R/spec_tools.R` in the workspace and of the browser lab, and into the class chart of the Multiverse page.
- [ ] **The file of Task 3.** The reproduction needs the file that Multi100 gave the analysts, which the workspace ships unchanged as `data/score_person_months.csv` (originally `Estimation Data - Kuo (JWzJ).csv`, osf.io/b6p3j). `check_score_file()` compares its MD5 sum with that of the copy on the OSF (`2b656d3814d273f4a93e29bc4f0139ef`). Nothing needs downloading on the day, and the browser lab loads the same file with the page.
- [ ] **Joining instructions.** Send the address of the track page, the setup page with the request to run `source("R/check_setup.R")` until it prints OK, the help page, and a reminder to bring a laptop and its charger. Ask the class to read **sections 1 and 2 of the case study only**: section 3 quotes the analyst who found what Task 3 asks the class to find, sections 4 to 6 describe it, and the day works best if most of the class finds it on the day.
- [ ] **The tab switching.** Click once through the sequence of Parts 3 and 4 (deck → specification menu and decision map → the Multiverse page and back), which is the one sequence that you run live several times in the day.
- [ ] **The room.** Confirm the projector, the power sockets, the wifi for visitors (the browser lab downloads its R engine, the union file and the file of the analysts, about 6 MB of data, on first load) and whether the room has Vevox or a similar response tool. The slides say "type in chat" for the five held answers of the day. In the room, decide in advance what "chat" means, from the options that the cue sheet below sets out.

### The night before

- [ ] Render the pages of the case and of the track page by page; never run a full `quarto render` of the project while pCloud syncs the folder, because it dies on renamed files. Check that the opening page, the track pages, the case pages and the deck are current, and push if the site is published.
- [ ] **The live-results loop.** Submit one test result from the browser lab (`try_spec()`, then `submit_exploration(nickname = "test-row")`), confirm that it reaches the Sheet with `cohabitation` after the tag, press *Run Code* on the class chart of the [Multiverse](../cases/cohabitation/multiverse.qmd#class-results) page and find the test circle. Then delete the test row from the Sheet.
- [ ] **The workspace, as a participant meets it.** Download the zip afresh, unzip it, open the folder in your IDE, run `source("R/check_setup.R")` (every line OK, the last at `r fmt(ref$b)`), render the report and check that Task 3 prints X-squared = `r fmt(an("5X3KG", "statistic_recorded"))` and Model 2 `r fmt(mark("OA_refit"))`, then complete the preregistration block with a dummy specification and render again.
- [ ] **The browser lab, cold.** Open the live page of the lab in a private window on a connection like that of the venue, time the load of the R engine and of the data, and run the setup cell (`r big(nrow(unions))` cohabitations, `r fmt(ref$b)`) and the Task 3 cell with the blanks filled (`r fmt(an("5X3KG", "statistic_recorded"))`).
- [ ] **The public record.** Confirm that the three addresses of the records slide load without an account: osf.io/kv38j, osf.io/u8x9s and osf.io/b69nv, and that the components of the five analysts are reachable from the last one, because it is the target of the three-minute search in Part 4.
- [ ] **The fallback zip.** Put the workspace zip on a USB stick, for anyone whose download fails in the room. The file of Task 3 is inside it.
- [ ] Prepare the catch-up card (below) as a ready-to-paste text, and charge everything.

### Opening the room

- [ ] Put the address of the course site, the browser lab and the cheatsheet on the screen or the whiteboard as people arrive, with the wifi details.
- [ ] Hand out the green and red sticky notes, or open the response tool, and say what each means: green, working; red, stuck.
- [ ] Keep four tabs ready: the deck, the [decision map](../cases/cohabitation/map.qmd), the [specification menu](../cases/cohabitation/menu.qmd) and the [Multiverse](../cases/cohabitation/multiverse.qmd) page.
- [ ] Ask who has read the case study beyond section 2. Those who have may already know what Task 3 finds; ask them, kindly, to keep it to themselves until the class has counted.
- [ ] If you record, announce it now and say what is and is not recorded.

## Run sheet – the one-day course

Times in the part tables are relative: 0:00 is the start of that part. The clock below maps them onto the day.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Draft clock times for CM to adjust.** The default below starts at 10:00 and keeps the breaks of the slides (thirty minutes, an hour, thirty minutes), so the day ends at 18:00. A 09:30 start ends at 17:30. Shorter breaks need the text of the break slides changed as well (`slides/_segments/shared/_break1.qmd`, `_lunch.qmd`, `_break2.qmd`), and those slides are shared by the decks of every case.
:::

| Segment | Elapsed | Example clock |
|---|---|---|
| Part 1 – Credibility and tools | 0:00–1:30 | 10:00–11:30 |
| Break | 1:30–2:00 | 11:30–12:00 |
| Part 2 – The claim, its estimand and its causal graph | 2:00–3:30 | 12:00–13:30 |
| Lunch | 3:30–4:30 | 13:30–14:30 |
| Part 3 – Reproduction and exploration | 4:30–6:00 | 14:30–16:00 |
| Break | 6:00–6:30 | 16:00–16:30 |
| Part 4 – Multiverse, replication and preregistration | 6:30–8:00 | 16:30–18:00 |

**Four stretches of the deck are optional**, marked on screen and switched in one keystroke: the five tools slides of Part 1, the R tutorial of Part 2 (nine slides), the methods tutorial of Part 3 (five slides on person-period data and discrete-time models) and the multiverse background of Part 4 (two slides). The timings below assume that you walk about half of each. Walking all of them in full costs about fifteen minutes that the day does not have, and skipping them all leaves the hands-on tasks more room than they need.

### Deck controls {#deck-controls}

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| space · right arrow · clicker | next slide, always exactly one: the deck is linear, so that no clicker press can skip a part |
| **`d`** | switch between the **extended** and the **lean** deck, live; in lean mode the optional slides are taken out of the deck and every key skips them |
| **`]`** and **`[`** | jump to the next or the previous part |
| **`g`** | jump bar: type a few letters of any slide title and press Enter |
| **`s`** | speaker view, with the notes, a timer and the next slide |
| **`f`** · **`esc`** | full screen · slide overview |

The readout at the top right names the part and the position, and its badge shows the state of the deck: green **extended**, burgundy **optional** on a slide of an optional run, amber **lean** when the runs are off, with a burgundy dot where a run has been lifted out. Adding `?depth=0` to the address opens the deck lean. The first slide of each optional run carries a small grey link that jumps to where the main flow resumes.

### Part 1 – Credibility and tools (90′)

| Rel. | Segment | What I do | What participants do | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0:00 | Welcome, the two kinds of aim, what you do not need (6′) | The premise in two sentences: *Nature* asked three times whether social science holds up, I was inside one of the papers, and today you sit where I sat. Walk the aims slide. "Open your workspace now." | Open the workspace in their IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), or the browser lab. | Late arrivals: a nod and the address on the screen, never a restart. |
| 0:06 | Talk: what social science is for, and why it is called a crisis (10′) | Claims and checking; false positives and forking paths; the evidence from replications; incentives and questionable research practices, and why the problem is structural rather than fraud. | Listen. | Say clearly that the problem is structural; it sets the tone for how the error of the afternoon is discussed. |
| 0:16 | Talk: the red-card study (4′) | The question, the design, and the twenty-nine estimates. | Watch. | The study returns in Part 2 as a single row, so tell it in full only here. |
| 0:20 | Talk: the vocabulary and open research (10′) | Replication crises; the data × analysis matrix; repeatability and credibility; the quick check, two slides, answered aloud; open-research practices. | Answer the quick check. | The matrix is the slide to copy down. If the segment runs long, the open-research table compresses to one sentence a row. |
| 0:30 | Talk: SCORE and its three studies (20′) | The programme; the three studies, each with its result; the three Rs across SCORE and why they do not travel together. | Listen. | If behind, cut the data-availability slide of Miske et al. to one line. Keep the quotation "reproducibility success does not mean that the finding is correct": Part 3 comes back to it. |
| 0:50 | Talk: Multi100 from the inside (8′) | What an analyst received, the two tasks, results on a common scale. | Listen. | The paper of the case and its five analysts come in Part 2; this segment presents Multi100 as a study. |
| 0:58 | Talk: the tools (18′) | Open source; the toolchain; plain-text formats and rendering; archives; the workspace and the browser lab; what the tools cannot do. Optional: languages, editors, packages, version control, licences. | Note what they might switch to. | The two slides to cover in full are plain-text formats and what the tools cannot do, which leads into Part 2. |
| 1:16 | Task 1 and the break (14′) | "Get to the point where a line of R runs and the data are in front of you; take the break for it if you need to." Circulate. Stay in the room through the break for red notes. | `source("R/check_setup.R")`, every line OK, the last at `r fmt(ref$b)`; or the setup cell of the lab. | This is the only point of the day where a broken machine can be fixed without costing anyone content. Anyone still stuck at the end of the break moves to the browser lab or to the zip on the USB stick. |

### Part 2 – The claim, its estimand and its causal graph (90′)

| Rel. | Segment | What I do | What participants do | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0:00 | Talk: the paper (16′) | Define the original authors (OAs) here. The question, the data and the unions, the life table, the model on person-months and its result, the finding by education, the claim. | Listen; ask. | Read the full sentence of the conclusions aloud, then the cut. Name the interaction in Model 2 now and leave its meaning for Part 3. |
| 0:16 | Talk: the five analysts (6′) | The table, then the three conclusions from one file and the quotation of N8ZYW. | Watch. | **Do not explain the split.** "Hold the question of why; you will answer it in Task 3." If someone who read ahead offers the answer, thank them and ask them to hold it until the class has counted. |
| 0:22 | Talk: estimands (12′) | Two studies beside our five; four estimands in the red-card study; the spread with and without a fixed estimand; under-specified questions; Lundberg's steps. | Listen. | The figure with and without a fixed estimand is the point of the segment. |
| 0:34 | Talk: the causal-graph crash course (14′) | Confounder, mediator, collider; the stories behind one correlation; open and closed paths; total and direct effects; selection and feedback. | Listen. | If running long, compress total and direct effects, **never selection**: it is the subject of the next segment. |
| 0:48 | Talk: the claim (16′) | The estimand statement and the first held answer: "write your statement, hold it, go"; read three or four aloud. Then who cohabits, the graph, the selection into cohabitation as conditioning on a collider, and the two readings of "cohabitors". | Write the statement; send on "go". | The held answer is never compressed. Do not settle which reading of "cohabitors" is right: the curve keeps all three adjustment sets for that reason, and they differ by about three hundredths. |
| 1:04 | R tutorial, optional (8′) | Walk as much as the least confident half of the class needs. | Follow. | The first thing to cut if the morning has overrun. |
| 1:12 | Hands-on 2: Task 2 (18′) | Counting, the composition of the cohorts, person-months and the life table, the estimand statement in the report, then `R/dag_starter.R`: the arrow of the claim, `adjustmentSets(dag)`, `paths(dag, Z = "cohabits")`, `paths(dag, Z = c("cohabits", "education", "race"))`, and the arrow from the period to the age at the start. | Count, write, finish the graph, two sentences. | At 1:22, if the class is behind, switch to demonstration: run it on the shared screen, and they finish over lunch. |
| 1:30 | Lunch | Post the return time. | Lunch. | A hard stop. |

### Part 3 – Reproduction and exploration (90′)

| Rel. | Segment | What I do | What participants do | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0:00 | Re-entry and the instruction (8′) | A visual sweep; the catch-up card on screen. The Task 2 instruction of Multi100 word for word, what it left open, and analyst no. 6. | Rejoin; latecomers follow the card. | Do not wait past 0:05. |
| 0:08 | Hands-on 3: Task 3, the reproduction (12′) | Drive the workspace on the shared screen beside them; circulate. Then the second held answer: "type your $\chi^2$, hold it, go". | Run `check_score_file()` and the chunk of the analyst; land on X-squared = `r fmt(an("5X3KG", "statistic_recorded"))`; send on "go". | The wall of identical values is the point of the beat, so wait until most of the class has a number (see the reproduction moment below). |
| 0:20 | The discovery (18′) | The shares behind the test; the question "how many unions and marriages does the file hold for 1995?"; Hands-on 3, the unions of the file, and the third held answer. Only then the file beside the rebuild, how the 1995 rows were built, the five analyses on a repaired file, and reproducibility and the file. | Count the unions of the file; send the count of 1995 unions and marriages on "go"; set them beside the paper. | **Let the class find it** (see the discovery moment below). Never show the slide of the file beside the rebuild before the counts are in chat. Tell the error without blame. |
| 0:38 | Task 3, second part: Model 2 (8′) | `fit_spec(unions, adjust = "race_period")` on the shared screen; then the coefficient beside an interaction. | Run the Model 2 chunk: `r fmt(mark("OA_refit"))`. | The point is the meaning of the coefficient: the change for non-Hispanic white women. Ask the class what the interaction of the race-ethnicity groups does before you show the table. |
| 0:46 | The menu (10′) | The fifteen decisions at three levels, the six that vary on the curve, the curve of 144, the ground rules. | Start choosing which decision interests them. | Point at the row of the union histories: the file of the analysts is on the menu, off the curve, as a weaker answer. |
| 0:56 | The methods (12′, part optional) | Weights and the survey design; the length of the whole union. Optional: person-period data, the monthly chance of marrying, the three discrete-time models, the time since the start, effect sizes on one scale. | Listen; ask. | The compressible segment: if Task 3 overran, take time from here, not from Task 4. |
| 1:08 | Hands-on 4: Task 4, exploring the menu (22′) | "Try several, read what each does, then submit the one you would defend." Suggest `try_spec(cohorts = "five_years")` for the largest move and `try_spec(histories = "score_file")` so that people read a refusal. Keep the Multiverse page on screen and press *Run Code* as the open circles land. | `try_spec()` three or four times; `my_experiments()`; `submit_exploration()`. | Everyone submits a mark, because Part 4 opens on them. Say twice that this is exploration and that Task 5 is the preregistered analysis. |
| 1:30 | Break | Leave the Multiverse page open. | Break. | – |

### Part 4 – Multiverse, replication and preregistration (90′)

| Rel. | Segment | What I do | What participants do | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0:00 | Your own small multiverse and the curve (10′) | Name what Task 4 was; optionally the origins and the garden of forking paths; then the curve of the claim, with the published result and 456AP placed on it. | Watch. | The published result sits among the smallest declines because it is the change for white women: connect it to Part 3. |
| 0:10 | The class multiverse and the placement (10′) | Refresh the class chart; the question bank (below). Then the fourth held answer: "rerun your submitted specification, read your placement, hold it, go". | Find their mark; read and send their placement. | Participants without a submission use the reference specification, whose placement is `r placement(ref$b)`. |
| 0:20 | What moved the estimate (8′) | The shifts by option, the curve coloured by the cohort window, what the curve leaves out. | Connect the window to their own choice. | The point of the last slide: the decision that reversed the Multi100 results lies upstream of every specification. |
| 0:28 | The replications (14′) | The SCORE replication and its coefficient; the claim on later surveys; the three Rs on this paper; what the repetitions found. | Listen; argue. | The last slide is the lesson of the day; never compress it. Keep it free of blame: careful people built the file, and the course found the error only because everything was public. |
| 0:42 | Critics and preregistration (8′) | The critics; one correct analysis and how to identify it; what preregistration settles; exploration against declaration. | Listen; ask. | If the clock is tight, the identification slide goes to one sentence. |
| 0:50 | Archiving and the public record (6′) | Archiving and registering; the Multi100 preregistration; the two templates; the records slide with the three-minute search of the Multi100 component; the eight AsPredicted questions. | Search the component; paste one decision in chat. | If time is short, show the search on the shared screen. |
| 0:56 | Hands-on 5: preregistration, run and report (26′) | Called from the front: complete fields 1–5, render or copy the cell, then the fifth held answer, "declared". Count aloud. Move on at about 80% declared or at ten minutes. Then `run_spec()` and `report_result()`; press *Run Code* as the filled circles land. | Declare, render, run, submit. | Never cut the declaration. Re-declaring a specification already explored is allowed, and the block must say so. |
| 1:22 | Close and feedback (8′) | Two points from the literature; the single analytical path; what you take with you; the feedback form, with the chart on screen. | Feedback. | End on time. |

## The held answers {#held-answers}

Five times in the day the class writes an answer, holds it and releases it together: the estimand statement (Part 2), the reproduced $\chi^2$ (Part 3), the count of the 1995 unions and marriages in the file (Part 3), the placement (Part 4) and "declared" before the preregistered run (Part 4). Holding the answers keeps each one independent of the others, and releasing them together is what produces the wall of identical values after the reproduction and the moment of surprise after the count. The slides say "type in chat"; the cue sheet below says what that means in the room.

**The reproduction moment.** Everyone runs `check_score_file()` and then the chunk of Task 3, which is the code of 5X3KG on the file that Multi100 gave the analysts. When most of the class has a number: "Type your $\chi^2$, hold it … go." The target is **X-squared = `r fmt(an("5X3KG", "statistic_recorded"))`** on one degree of freedom, from `r sr(1, "married")` marriages in `r big(sr(1, "rows"))` rows of 1995 and `r sr(0, "married")` in `r big(sr(0, "rows"))` rows of 2006–2010, the value recorded for 5X3KG. The usual departures, and what they mean:

- **A $\chi^2$ of `r fmt(chi_uncorrected, 2)`.** The participant left out the continuity correction (`correct = FALSE`), which the analyst kept. Say so and move on; the shares are the same.
- **A $\chi^2$ of `r fmt(an("5X3KG", "stat_repaired"), 2)`.** The participant ran ahead to the optional extension of the task, the same test with the 1995 rows rebuilt. Ask them to hold that number until the class has counted, because it belongs to the discussion that follows the count.
- **An error in the browser lab** that mentions unexpected input. The blanks of the code of a marriage are still `______`; they take the value 2, and the hint below the cell says so.
- **`check_score_file()` reports a mismatch.** A file in `data/` was opened and saved by a spreadsheet program. Copy `data/score_person_months.csv` from the zip on the USB stick, or carry on in the browser lab.

**The discovery moment.** This is the beat that the day is built around, and its force comes from the class finding the error rather than being told. After the reproduction, show the slide of the shares behind the test and let the class read it: the test says that marriage became about fourteen times more common, the opposite of the claim. Then ask, and only ask: "The paper reports 340 marriages among its 929 unions of 1990–1995. How many unions, and how many marriages, does the file hold for 1995?" Put up the slide of the unions of the file, ask everyone to run the next chunk of the report before reading the text below it, and wait. The chunk `score-unions` of Task 3 in the report gives the counts, and the paragraph after the next chunk gives the explanation, so participants who read ahead will have it. Ask them to hold it. When most of the class has a count: "Type the number of unions of 1995 and the number of marriages, hold … go." The target is **`r su("1995", "intact") + su("1995", "marriage") + su("1995", "separation")` unions: `r su("1995", "intact")` intact, `r su("1995", "marriage")` marriages, `r su("1995", "separation")` separations**, against 929: 242, 340 and 347 in the paper. Let the counts sit on screen for a moment, and give the class a minute to propose what could produce them before you advance; the next two slides give the answer. Of the 929 unions, the file holds `r kept("separation")` of the separations, `r kept("marriage")` of the marriages and `r kept("intact")` of the intact unions.

Usual departures at this moment: a participant who reports `r big(sr(1, "rows"))` has counted rows, not unions; point them at `slice_max(MONTHNUM, n = 1, by = CASEID)`, which keeps the last month of each union. A participant who reports 1,150 unions has read the line of 2006–2010, which is close to the 1,142 of the paper; ask for the line of 1995.

How to tell it. The data dictionary of the SCORE replication builds the length of a 1995 union as "STOPOTH0 - STRTOTH0", the month in which the woman stopped living with her first former partner minus the month in which she began; the rule is right for almost every union that dissolved, and a union that became a marriage or was still intact has no stop date and drops out. Say that the rule was sensible, that the file was built by careful people, that one analyst of five (456AP) found the gap by counting first, and that every step of the discovery was possible only because the survey, the file, its dictionary and the scripts were public. The names of the SCORE team appear in the fact sheet of the case and nowhere in the materials; keep it that way in the room.

**The catch-up card**, for the re-entry to Part 3:

> Just back? You have missed nothing that you cannot recover: (1) if Task 2 is unfinished, run the graph chunk as it stands and come back to the wording later; (2) Task 3 is the reproduction – the target is X-squared = 47.474, the code is on the slide and in your report, and the file is already in `data/`; please do not read past the reproduction chunk in your report until we have counted together; (3) Task 4 is exploration, so try two specifications and submit one. Put up a red note and I will come to you during Task 4.

## In person and online {#cue-sheet}

The materials are the same in both settings. What changes is how people answer, flag trouble and pair up.

| Beat | In person | Online |
|---|---|---|
| Held answers | the response tool of the room if it has one; otherwise written on a card and held up on "go" | typed in chat, sent on "go" |
| Working or stuck | green and red sticky notes on the laptop lid | a green circle or "STUCK" in chat |
| Rescues | the facilitator circulates | the problem shown on the shared screen |
| The live chart | on the projector, and on the laptops | everyone opens the Multiverse page |
| Form links | on the screen | pasted in chat |
| Breaks | the countdown slide and the time aloud | the countdown slide and "back at :xx" in chat |

## The cutting order {#cutting-order}

When time runs short, cut from the optional runs before anything else, so that the time comes out of a tutorial before it comes out of a task.

- **Part 1** – at 0:30, cut the data-availability slide of Miske et al. to one line and the open-research table to one sentence a row. At 0:58, leave the optional tools run switched off.
- **Part 2** – at 0:34, take total and direct effects in one sentence. At 1:04, skip the R tutorial. At 1:22, Task 2 becomes a demonstration, finished over lunch.
- **Part 3** – at 0:46, the ground rules go to one sentence. At 0:56, the methods run stays off and the length of the whole union goes to one sentence. At 1:08, Task 4 shortens to two calls of `try_spec()` and a submission, but everybody still submits.
- **Part 4** – at 0:00, skip the multiverse background. At 0:20, take what the curve leaves out in one sentence. At 0:50, show the three-minute search on the shared screen instead of setting it.

**Never cut:** the three conclusions from one file · the held estimand statement · the selection into cohabitation · the reproduction and its held answer · the count of the 1995 unions, before the figure · Model 2 and the coefficient beside an interaction · the Task 4 submission · what the repetitions found · the preregistration moment.

## Fallbacks {#fallbacks}

Each row names the first move, not the only one, and every ladder ends at a point from which the session can carry on.

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| **An installation fails on the day** | The browser lab holds the whole exercise and gives the same numbers, the reproduction of Task 3 included; the participant carries on there, and the workspace survives for later. |
| **The workspace download fails in the room** | The zip on the USB stick, which holds the file of Task 3 as well. |
| **The OSF is down** | Nothing in Tasks 1–5 needs it, because the file of the analysts ships with the workspace and the lab. Only the three-minute search of Part 4 does; show the records slide and describe the components instead. |
| **The browser lab stalls** | The ladder of the [cheatsheet](../cases/cohabitation/cheatsheet.qmd): a hard reload and the cells above run again, then a second browser, then the shared screen, then the by-hand lookup, in which the facilitator reads the six choices off `spec_curve.csv` and submits the row through the Form. Everyone still gets a mark. |
| **The wifi fails** | The workspace runs offline once its packages are installed, so Tasks 1–5 continue; only the submissions wait. Collect the printed results (the tag, the label, `b`, `se`, `t`, `df`, `n`, `r`) and submit them through the Form when the network returns. The browser lab needs the network for its first load. |
| **The live chart fails** (Form, Worker, CORS) | The chart falls back to the committed `cases/cohabitation/data/class_results.csv`, which holds only its header. Pull the Sheet as CSV, keep the rows that carry `cohabitation` after the tag, put them in place of that file, render the Multiverse page locally and share the screen. The static curve and the reference marks at the top of the page are enough for the debrief. Submissions are safe in the Sheet whatever happens to the chart. |
| **A participant has lost their tag** | It is in `.class-tag` at the root of the workspace; in the lab, `report_result(nickname = "their-tag")` reuses it. |

## Expected numbers {#expected-numbers}

- **Task 1.** The last check of `R/check_setup.R`: the reference specification reproduces at `r fmt(ref$b)` on the log scale; the lab prints the same, with `r big(nrow(unions))` cohabitations.
- **Task 2.** `r big(nrow(unions))` first premarital cohabitations in five surveys; in the window of the paper `r big(sum(paper$cycle == "1995"))` unions of 1995 (`r oc("1995", "marriage")` marriages, `r oc("1995", "separation")` separations, `r oc("1995", "intact")` intact) and `r big(sum(paper$cycle == "2006-10"))` of 2006–2010 (`r oc("2006-10", "marriage")`, `r oc("2006-10", "separation")`, `r oc("2006-10", "intact")`). Weighted shares, 1990–1995 against 2005–2010: Hispanic `r pct(share("1995", \(d) d$race == "hispanic"))` and `r pct(share("2006-10", \(d) d$race == "hispanic"))`, Black `r pct(share("1995", \(d) d$race == "black"))` and `r pct(share("2006-10", \(d) d$race == "black"))`, college degree `r pct(share("1995", \(d) d$educ == "college"))` and `r pct(share("2006-10", \(d) d$educ == "college"))`; mean age at the start `r fmt(share("1995", \(d) d$age_start), 1)` in both. `r big(sum(paper$duration + 1))` person-months, `r sum(paper$outcome == "marriage")` of them ending in a marriage. The life table at month 36: `r pct(lt36$married[lt36$cohort == "1990-1995"])` married in 1990–1995 against `r pct(lt36$married[lt36$cohort == "2005-2010"])` in 2005–2010 (the paper quotes 41% and 24%). The graph: `adjustmentSets(dag)` returns the empty set, because nothing in the graph causes the period; `paths(dag)` lists three paths through `cohabits`, all closed; under `Z = "cohabits"` all three are open, and with education and race-ethnicity held constant as well they close again.
- **Task 3, the reproduction.** X-squared = `r fmt(an("5X3KG", "statistic_recorded"))` on 1 df from `r sr(1, "married")` of `r big(sr(1, "rows"))` rows of 1995 and `r sr(0, "married")` of `r big(sr(0, "rows"))` rows of 2006–2010 (`r big(an("5X3KG", "n_recorded"))` rows). The unions of the file: 1995, `r su("1995", "intact")` intact, `r su("1995", "marriage")` marriages and `r su("1995", "separation")` separations; 2006–2010, `r su("2006-10", "intact")`, `r su("2006-10", "marriage")` and `r su("2006-10", "separation")`. Of the 929 unions of 1995 in the paper, the file holds `r kept("separation")` of the 347 separations, `r kept("marriage")` of the 340 marriages and `r kept("intact")` of the 242 intact unions. The extension with the 1995 rows rebuilt: $\chi^2$ = `r fmt(an("5X3KG", "stat_repaired"), 2)`, less marriage in the later rows.
- **Task 3, Model 2.** `fit_spec(unions, adjust = "race_period")`: `r fmt(mark("OA_refit"))` (SE `r fmt(mark("OA_refit", "se"))`) against the published −0.683 (0.14). The changes by race-ethnicity in Model 2: `r fmt(sg("race_period", "white"), 2)` for non-Hispanic white women, `r fmt(sg("race_period", "black"), 2)` for Black women, `r fmt(sg("race_period", "hispanic"), 2)` for Hispanic women, `r fmt(sg("race_period", "other"), 2)` for the other group.
- **The reference specification** (the window of the paper, every observed month, age, race-ethnicity and education, weighted, months since the start as a straight line, multinomial logit): `r fmt(ref$b)`, SE `r fmt(ref$se)`, *t* = `r fmt(ref$stat, 2)` on `r ref$df` df with design-based errors, a ratio of `r fmt(ref$ratio, 2)`, partial *r* = `r fmt(ref$r)`, on `r big(ref$n)` person-months of `r big(ref$n_unions)` unions.
- **The curve.** `r nrow(curve)` specifications, all below zero and all significant at 5% with design-based errors, from `r fmt(min(curve$b))` to `r fmt(max(curve$b))` (ratios `r fmt(min(curve$ratio), 2)` to `r fmt(max(curve$ratio), 2)`); the design-based *t* runs from `r fmt(min(curve$stat), 2)` to `r fmt(max(curve$stat), 2)`. Mean by adjustment set: none `r fmt(bs("none"))`, age `r fmt(bs("age"))`, age, race-ethnicity and education `r fmt(bs("composition"))`. Mean shifts against twins: the same window in both surveys `r sgn(shift("cohorts", "five_years"))`, no weights `r sgn(shift("weights", "unweighted"))`, age, race-ethnicity and education `r sgn(shift("adjust", "composition"))`; every other option less than 0.015. The cohort window carries `r round(100 * var_part("cohorts"))`% of the variance of the estimates and the weights `r round(100 * var_part("weights"))`%. No option changes a verdict.
- **Placement** (specifications further below zero). The reference specification `r placement(ref$b)` of `r nrow(curve)`; `try_spec(cohorts = "five_years")` `r placement(five_years_ref$b)`; the published result `r placement(mark("OA"))`; 456AP `r placement(mark("456AP"))`.
- **The reference marks.** OAs 2016 `r fmt(mark("OA"))`; Model 2 refitted `r fmt(mark("OA_refit"))`; 456AP `r fmt(mark("456AP"))` (2002 against 2013–2015, z = `r fmt(mark("456AP", "stat"), 2)`); the SCORE replication, some college × period, `r fmt(mark("SCORE_replication"))` (`r pe(mark("SCORE_replication", "p"))`); the SCORE "reproduction dataset" `r fmt(mark("SCORE_reproduction"))` (its script gives p = `r fmt(mark("SCORE_reproduction", "p"), 4)`, its report 0.02484); the course on 2002 against 2011–2015 `r fmt(mark("course_2002_2011"))`, on 1995 against 2011–2015 `r fmt(mark("course_1995_2011"))`.
- **Inference at the reference specification.** Design-based SE `r fmt(inf("design", "se"))`, *t* = `r fmt(inf("design", "stat"), 2)` on `r inf("design", "df")` df; clustered by woman `r fmt(inf("woman", "se"))`, *t* = `r fmt(inf("woman", "stat"), 2)` on `r big(inf("woman", "df"))` df; conventional `r fmt(inf("model", "se"))`, *z* = `r fmt(inf("model", "stat"), 2)`.
- **Options off the curve, at the reference settings.** Model 2 `r fmt(opt("adjust", "race_period"))`; Model 1 `r fmt(opt("adjust", "educ_period"))` (`r pe(opt("adjust", "educ_period", "p"))`); the total length of the union `r fmt(opt("adjust", "total_duration"))`; no time term `r fmt(opt("time", "none"), 4)`; education as in the SCORE file `r fmt(opt("education", "score"))`; very short unions kept `r fmt(opt("short", "keep"))`; the linear probability model `r fmt(opt("model", "lpm"), 4)`; 2002 against 2006–2010 `r fmt(opt("comparison", "2002_2006"))` (`r pe(opt("comparison", "2002_2006", "p"))`); 2006–2010 against 2011–2015 `r fmt(opt("comparison", "2006_2011"))` (`r pe(opt("comparison", "2006_2011", "p"))`).
- **The five analysts.** Task 1 of Multi100: 73FDT and 456AP evidence for the claim, JDA15 evidence neither way, N8ZYW and 5X3KG evidence for the opposite. On the file of the analysts and with its 1995 rows rebuilt: N8ZYW *z* = `r sgn(an("N8ZYW", "stat_refit"), 2)` and `r fmt(an("N8ZYW", "stat_repaired"), 2)`; JDA15 *z* = `r fmt(an("JDA15", "stat_refit"), 2)` and `r fmt(an("JDA15", "stat_repaired"), 2)`; 73FDT *F* = `r fmt(an("73FDT", "stat_refit"), 2)` and `r fmt(an("73FDT", "stat_repaired"), 2)`; 456AP unchanged.

## Debrief questions {#debrief}

Choose by what the class chart shows, not by the order below.

1. **The windows.** "Who took the same five-year window in both surveys, and why did the decline shrink? Which window answers the claim as you read it?"
2. **The weights.** "Every Multi100 analyst had to work without weights. What population does an unweighted estimate describe here, and does the claim say which it means?"
3. **Justification.** "Whose causal graph settled their choice of adjustment? Who would defend the change for cohabitors as they were, the change in who cohabits included?"
4. **The exact reproduction.** "The class reproduced a number to the third decimal, and the number pointed the wrong way. What would you check, and in what order, before trusting a file that you did not build?"
5. **The coefficient of the claim.** "The number that Multi100 attached to the claim is the change for white women. How would you have noticed that from the paper alone?"
6. **Two replications.** "SCORE reported 'not replicated' for a coefficient that the analysts were told to leave out. What should a reader of the verdict be told?"
7. **Placement.** "Your placement puts you among 144 justifiable alternatives, all of them below zero. What does a curve like this one say, and what can it not say about the file on which it was built?"
8. **How preregistration felt.** "Did writing the block before running change how the result felt when it landed? Would you have chosen differently after the exploration?"
